description: The communication layer between people and robots, and between robots. Talk to any robot in your own words, with an LLM for its brain. Robots that have never met check each other's passports and share the work. Microduck, Huebot, Open Duck Mini, LeRobot arms, XLeRobot carts, AlohaMini, ToddlerBot, MOSS, ROS bases and industrial arms on ROS 2.

latest_release.body:
## The arm on LeRobot 0.7.0

LeRobot 0.7.0 replaced `feetech-servo-sdk`, the library under the SO-101's bus, with rustypot, one
`SerialMotorsBus` for every Feetech and Dynamixel servo. `quackd[lerobot]` installs LeRobot 0.7.0 now,
below 0.7.1, with rustypot below 1.14, and every LeRobot name the arm relies on was read again at the
`v0.7.0` tag, with the bus below LeRobot's Python at rustypot's `v1.13.1`.

What the arm says changed with the bus. A failed torque call names every joint it could not switch,
so `connect attempt 1 of 3 failed on elbow_flex (id 3) and gripper (id 6): ...` sends you to both
cables. A release over motors that do not answer gets the time LeRobot 0.7.0 takes, a panic in
rustypot is met as a failed bus call, and a second program on the arm's port is refused as it opens
it, on Linux and macOS too. `quackd robot release`, and a `--by-hand` run that opened the gripper,
close it before they let go of the arm.

`lerobot:mock` runs the real backend's own code over an arm in memory, so a rehearsal on it refuses,
hands off and closes in the arm's own words.

## Industrial arms on ROS 2

`quackd[rosarm]` installs the tenth adapter, `quackd-rosarm`, for a Universal Robots UR5e, a KUKA LBR
iisy 3 R760 or LBR iiwa 7 R800, or a Yaskawa MotoMini, each behind a ROS 2 driver, its maker's for
three of them and the LBR-Stack for the iiwa, and rosbridge. A move is one goal to every joint, inside
the travel the arm's own description gives and at most a tenth of each joint's rated speed, and every
move asks a person first
([ADR-0078](https://github.com/rokbenko/quackd/blob/v0.34.0/docs/adr/0078-an-industrial-arm-is-moved-one-confirmed-goal-at-a-time.md)).
quackd never powers, enables, un-brakes or un-stops an arm, parks none and drives no tool.

`rosarm:mock` rehearses it over a fake rosbridge and a fake of each arm's driver, and `rosarm:ws`
refuses every arm until somebody names an owner and a date for its first run. A workflow in CI,
`rosarm contract`, runs the transport against rosbridge_server on Jazzy and Humble with a stand-in for
the arm's driver
([the industrial arm's page](https://github.com/rokbenko/quackd/blob/v0.34.0/docs/adapters/rosarm/README.md)).
A Universal Robots UR7e joins the described bodies beside the UR5e.

## A body's load, a key held down and a heartbeat on 3.11

A body can say what rides on its back or deck, `carries_kg`, and a task can ask for it
([ADR-0079](https://github.com/rokbenko/quackd/blob/v0.34.0/docs/adr/0079-what-rides-on-a-bodys-back-is-a-figure-and-an-unset-one-is-not-on-the-wire.md)).
A key held down, or an Enter read late by a key thread that a busy machine held up, no longer answers
yes to a question that drops an arm. A run on Python 3.11 ends though its heartbeat's cancel was lost.

## The policy server

The policy server reads LeRobot 0.7.0. It loads nothing where the `kernels` package is installed,
refuses a pinned model whose config would run a kernel from the Hub and a GR00T whose VLM step names
no model, and fetches a GR00T base pinned at a tag at the commit its `config.json` was read at.

## What changes for you

* `quackd[lerobot]` installs LeRobot 0.7.0 and rustypot, which Python 3.14 on Linux builds from
  source.
* A second program on the arm's port is refused on Linux and macOS too, so close whatever holds it
  before a run.
* `quackd robot release`, and a `--by-hand` run that opened the gripper, close it before they let go
  of the arm.
* `quackd_lerobot.real.load_policy()` is gone.
* `list-adapters --json` and `doctor --json` say `"extra": null` for a row no package installs, where
  they said `"built-in"`.
* Pillow 13 is quackd's own floor.
* The policy server refuses a SmolVLA, pi05, pi0 or X-VLA checkpoint that LeRobot 0.7.0 saved, for
  now, and loads nothing where `kernels` is installed, so `uv pip uninstall kernels` in its
  environment if it is there.

## What has not run

No arm has run quackd on LeRobot 0.7.0. The SO-101 last ran it on 2026-11-06, under quackd

Roboglot

Talk to your robots. Let them talk to each other.
Roboglot is the communication layer between people and robots, and between robots themselves. Say what you want in your own words, from a terminal, a page or Claude, and an LLM flies the robot. Robots that have never met check each other's passports, then divide the work. It began as the brain daemon the Microduck was missing. Ten robots today, one of them driven on real hardware and the other nine so far only on a mock, and one of them a duck you can print and build yourself. More are described from their makers' figures and not driven at all.

Register each robot once, by name. Then state a goal from a terminal, the page or a chat with Claude, to one robot or to a team of them, and the same contract decides which of each robot's skills its LLM may use, how many steps it gets, and when it has to ask you first.

Hey, my name is Rok and this is why I built Roboglot 👋 > I see Roboglot as a ChatGPT like moment for robotics. Let me explain what I mean. > > LLMs existed long before ChatGPT. What ChatGPT actually did was take LLMs and hand them to ordinary people in a chat interface everyone already knew, like Facebook Messenger or Instagram. That was the real unlock. > > Right now, in 2026, most people still think robots belong in science fiction movies or in a lab at Tesla. That is not true anymore. There are already open source robots you can build yourself for under $1000. And they actually work. They can go to your fridge, open it, grab a can of Coke, close the fridge and bring it to you. > > The problem is they have a huge limitation. You can teach them dozens of moves, like "get a coke". But the robot itself is still dumb. It knows the moves, it just cannot connect them on its own. For robots to become truly useful, they need to become AI first and agentic. You give them a goal and they figure out the steps themselves. > > To get there, robots need a brain. And here is the catch. Today's robots simply do not have enough hardware on board to think, reason and plan. Their skull is too small for the brain this kind of intelligence needs. So the brain has to live outside the robot, in the cloud or on your own computer, where it can grow as big as you need. The robot itself stays small and light while all the heavy thinking happens somewhere else. That is what Roboglot started as. A brain for one robot. > > But here is what I think comes next. In the future everyone will have a team of robots. At home, in the office, wherever. And they will not all be the same robot. Different types, different capabilities, even different companies. The first challenge is having all of them in ONE place to command. That is what Roboglot is now. You connect every robot you own to one CLI, and you command all of them from there, with an LLM as the brain of each one. > > But even when you have them all in one place, that is still not enough. What you ask for will be complex, and robots will probably be very specialized. One can walk, one can grab, one can carry. For a bunch of different robots to be useful with as little of your involvement as possible, they need to start working together towards the goals you give them. Which means they need to communicate between each other. So that is the other half of Roboglot. You give the team a goal, each robot's brain reads what the others can do, and they divide the work between themselves. > > Imagine telling your robots "I want to eat and drink something". The one with wheels goes to the fridge, checks what is inside and tells the others what it found. The one with arms grabs a plate and some cutlery. One of them brings it all to you and asks what you would like, you choose, and they go back for the food and wish you a good meal. Sounds like science fiction, right? We are closer than you think! > > That is basically what ChatGPT did for LLMs. It took something powerful and put it in one place everyone could reach. And that is why I see Roboglot as a ChatGPT like moment for robotics. > > — Rok Benko, September 2026


A real arm, a real LLM, one sentence. An SO-101 follower arm on 2026-09-15, piloted by OpenAI's gpt-6-astra through roboglot run --goal "Wave to the camera with an extended arm". The LLM was handed the arm's five verbs and its datasheet and chose one call at a time: raise the shoulder and elbow, roll the wrist four times, return, stop. Nobody wrote a wave. The whole run at ten times speed, filmed on a phone: it opens on the command going into a terminal, watches the run scroll, then pans to the bench, and the wave itself is the part where the wrist rocks. What the LLM was told, all ten of its calls and what went wrong are in What happened in that run, and how every recording here was made is in docs/assets.

**Roboglot** is the communication layer between people and the robots they own, and between those robots. Each one joins through an adapter that declares, as a manifest, what the body is and what it can do, and you register it once by name with how to reach it. Give a robot a goal like *"find the ball and kick it"* and an LLM picks one skill at a time from the list that manifest declares, Roboglot runs it, looks at the camera, and asks again until the job is done or clearly impossible. Give the same goal to a team and every robot in it gets an LLM of its own, and they divide the work by telling each other what they are going to do. A goal can arrive from a chat, a command line or a `.glot` task file, and whichever way it comes, Roboglot enforces a contract the pilot LLM cannot talk its way out of: which skills are allowed, how many steps, when a human must say yes, when to abort. Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, Grok, Mistral, DeepSeek, Cohere, Qwen, Kimi, GLM and Meta work over their APIs, and so do the LLMs OpenRouter routes to, behind one key of its own. Open source LLMs work on your own machine through Ollama, vLLM, llama.cpp or LM Studio, with no key. An LLM is the pilot on every run but a scripted one. `--decision-llm` optionally puts something in front of it that is **not** a pilot LLM and cannot be used as one: a decision LLM generates no text at all, it scores a fixed set of options against a state and returns which one with a probability for each, so it answers the turns that are a choice among calls the robot already has and can no more write a joint angle than a thermometer can. TypeSafe's Jev was the first of them and is hosted, OpenAI's Decisions API is the other hosted one, and the rest Roboglot names are open servers you run yourself or a checkpoint loaded into this process, each with a page of its own. Off unless you name one, and `--decision-mode shadow` records what one would have chosen without letting it change a thing ([docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md](docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md)). On the SO-101 arm a learned policy from Hugging Face's Hub, NVIDIA's GR00T and Physical Intelligence's pi0 among them, can drive the arm for one short segment at a time, and [Which models work](#which-models-work) lists every one of all three kinds and how to name each one. The first robot is the [Microduck](https://pollen-robotics.com/microduck/) from Pollen Robotics: a 25 cm, 800 g biped with fifteen small servos, a camera in its head, a depth sensor, a speaker and an onboard computer, open source and about $399, which already knows how to walk, turn, kick, scoop something off the floor, look around and quack at 50 Hz on its own hardware. It is the robot Roboglot started on, independently and unofficially. Nine more bodies follow it through adapters that declare what each can do: an [Open Duck Mini v2](https://github.com/apirrone/Open_Duck_Mini) you can print and build yourself, an SO-101 class arm through LeRobot, any wheeled base over rosbridge, an XLeRobot dual-arm cart, an AlohaMini with two arms on a lift, a ToddlerBot humanoid, a [Huebot](https://ce-net.com/huebot), a 25 cm biped with behaviour code of its own, whose maker is writing a shim for it that is to answer the Microduck's calls the same way, [MOSS](https://github.com/metrox-eth/moss), a small tracked rover that picks up litter, reached through its own cockpit and a bridge Roboglot ships for it, and an industrial arm on ROS 2 (a Universal Robots UR5e, a KUKA LBR iisy, a KUKA LBR iiwa or a Yaskawa MotoMini) through its ROS 2 driver and rosbridge, which only rehearses so far: its real backend is refused until somebody names a date for a first run on one. **One of the ten bodies runs on real hardware, and the recording above is it.** On 2026-09-15 an SO-101 follower arm ran Roboglot over `lerobot:real` through twelve `--goal` runs in one afternoon, piloted by OpenAI's `gpt-6-astra` from a Windows laptop with a USB webcam: it waved with its wrist, reached out with its shoulder and elbow, opened and closed its gripper, and once mimed a duck quacking with it. The GIF is the last of the twelve, and [What happened in that run](#what-happened-in-that-run) reads its transcript call by call. The honest half is there too. The arm fell at the end of every one of those runs, because LeRobot drops torque when it disconnects, which is what [the rest pose](#your-robots-by-name) was written afterwards to stop, and the camera framed the gripper and cropped the raised arm, so the LLM checked its own waves against joint readings rather than against the picture. On 2026-09-23 the same arm ran again, registered as `arm-01` with a rest pose, through 26 runs on Roboglot 0.12.0, and 23 of them came from ten task files written for that afternoon, which now sit among the 246 in [docs/examples/lerobot/](docs/examples/lerobot/README.md). Its rest pose could not reach a fold that lay past the travel its calibration recorded, 19 of the 26 runs never moved the arm at a pilot's request, and what Roboglot changed in answer has not run on an arm yet. The other nine bodies have not met hardware. Their real backends speak names read from upstream source at a pinned commit and have only ever talked to fakes, and for the Open Duck Mini and the ToddlerBot those fakes are the daemons Roboglot itself ships for the robot, exercised over loopback, so there only the body is untested. MOSS's bridge is Roboglot's own too, exercised the same way beside a fake of MOSS's cockpit. The industrial arm's fakes are written from reading each driver's source, and its real backend refuses to start until somebody names a date for a first run on an arm. No team has yet crossed from one machine to a second. Goals like *"find my keys"*, handed to a team that sorts out who does what, are where this is going, not what it does yet. The honest label for today is *LLM driven, goal directed control of one real arm and nine mocked bodies, alone or in teams*, and [Which robots work](#which-robots-work) says exactly how far each one has got. **No robot yet? You can still try it, on a mock.** Every adapter has a `mock` backend, an in-memory test double that stands in for its robot: it takes every intent, answers with a state from a script and, for a body with a camera, draws frames of its own. A run on a mock shows the contract, the gates and the command line working, and it shows nothing about how a robot behaves, because nothing a mock reports was measured on one. [No robot yet? Try it in 60 seconds](#no-robot-yet-try-it-in-60-seconds) has a command that runs on one, and what it printed.

## Quickstart: a LeRobot SO-101 arm Two ways to drive the same arm, and the steps that set the arm up are shared between them. **[From the terminal](#from-the-terminal)** is the path the recording at the top of this page took, in ten steps, with the arm calibrated, named and parked before anything you type can move it. **[From Claude, over MCP](#from-claude-over-mcp)** is the same arm reached from a chat instead, where the LLM you are already talking to is the pilot. Either way you need the arm and its serial port, a USB webcam, and Python 3.12 or newer, because LeRobot itself needs it. Only the terminal path needs a key for one cloud vendor, because only that one brings an LLM of its own. ### From the terminal 1. **Install the arm and a pilot into one environment.** Below Python 3.12 the `lerobot` extra resolves to nothing while the install still reports success, so pin the interpreter. ```bash uv venv --python 3.12 uv pip install "roboglot[lerobot,openai]" # or anthropic, gemini, grok, and so on ``` 2. **Put the key where Roboglot reads it.** One line in a `.env` file, in the folder you run from or in the venv root: `OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...`. `roboglot doctor` prints the key it found for each provider, masked to its ends, which is the quickest way to see that the file was read at all. 3. **Find the port, then calibrate under the name you will register.** Calibration is LeRobot's own tool and it asks you to move each joint through its range by hand. Take each one all the way into the fold you will rest the arm in, because the travel it records is written into the servos as limits they are never driven past, and a fold outside it is a pose the arm cannot be driven back to. Roboglot reads every joint limit out of the file it writes, and refuses an arm that has none. ```bash lerobot-find-port lerobot-calibrate --robot.type=so101_follower --robot.port=COM3 --robot.id=arm-01 ``` 4. **First contact, which moves nothing.** Connect, read the joints, temperatures and torque back, disconnect. Support the arm while it starts, because connecting releases torque for a moment. A spec on its own carries no name, so it reads the calibration saved as `arm-01` whatever name you calibrated under. If you chose another, do step 5 first and run `roboglot doctor --robot` with that name instead, which reads the calibration kept under it. ```bash roboglot doctor --robot lerobot:real --address COM3 ``` 5. **Name it.** The registry keeps the port, the camera and the pilot under one name, so every command after this is `--robot arm-01`. Register it under the id you calibrated as. ```bash roboglot robot add arm-01 lerobot:real --address COM3 --llm openai:gpt-6-astra ``` 6. **Fold the arm by hand, then record where it rests.** An SO-101 has no brake and LeRobot releases torque when it disconnects, so without this the arm would drop from wherever a run left it, and Roboglot refuses to run it at all. With it, every run starts at this pose and returns to it before Roboglot lets go. This pose is where every run starts and ends unless the run itself says otherwise, and the one flag that says otherwise is just below step 10, where it changes the start and leaves the end alone. If it warns that a joint is recorded past what this calibration lets its servo be driven to, your fold lies outside the travel step 3 recorded: a run parks that joint at the edge of its travel and lets it settle from there, and calibrating again with the joint taken all the way into the fold, then recording the pose again, makes the fold itself reachable. Record the pose again after any new calibration too, because a calibration can move a joint's zero and the pose is kept as angles. ```bash roboglot robot rest-pose arm-01 ``` 7. **The first task moves nothing either.** `lerobot-lookout` allows `report_state` and `stop` and nothing else: it reads the arm and says what it found. There is nothing to improvise, so the scripted pilot is enough and this costs no tokens. ```bash roboglot run lerobot-lookout --robot arm-01 --llm fake ``` 8. **Add the webcam.** `lerobot-find-cameras opencv` prints the indices and saves a frame from each, so you can see which is which. Point it at the space the arm moves through rather than at the gripper, which is the mistake the run above made. ```bash roboglot robot edit arm-01 --camera-url "opencv://2" ``` 9. **Rehearse it.** With `--dry-run` the arm is connected and read, and not one command reaches it, so you see which verbs the LLM reaches for and with what numbers before a joint moves. ```bash roboglot run --goal "Wave to the camera with an extended arm" --robot arm-01 --max-steps 10 --dry-run ``` 10. **Then let it move.** A hand near the power switch, the arm's whole sweep clear, and the same sentence without the flag. This run starts at the rest pose you recorded in step 6 and folds back to it when it is over, which is the default and the first of the two choices below rather than the only way a run can begin. If the arm cannot get back to its rest pose at the end, the run says it is holding itself up and asks you to clear whatever is in its way and press Enter, and it tries the fold once more. Only if that fold misses too does it ask again, and Enter at that second question takes torque off where the arm stands, so the arm drops: hold it first. Leave either question for 60 seconds and torque stays on. After that, `roboglot robot release arm-01` folds the arm to its rest pose and lets go of it there, asking the same two questions if its fold misses: support the arm while it connects, because connecting takes torque off for a moment, then take your hands away when it says so, in the 3 seconds it waits before it folds. None of this has run on a real arm yet. ```bash roboglot run --goal "Wave to the camera with an extended arm" --robot arm-01 --max-steps 10 ``` **Or start from a pose you set by hand.** `--by-hand` gives you the arm before the pilot gets it. The arm is driven to the rest pose from step 6 first, torque comes off there, and Roboglot waits: lift the arm, put whatever the task needs into the gripper, close the gripper on it, hold the arm where the run should begin, and press Enter. Lift it out of its fold before you press Enter, even where the run should begin next to it, because a fold that lies past the travel step 3 recorded is let go of at the edge of that travel and is free to settle back past it. Roboglot writes the pose you left as the goal, puts torque back on, reads the joints again to check nothing sagged, and prints the angles it is now holding so you know you can let go. The pilot works from there. A joint outside its calibrated travel when you press Enter is the exception, whether you placed it there or never lifted it out of the fold: nothing can hold it where it is, so torque stays off, Roboglot names the joint and its travel, and the run ends with the arm limp, in your hands or still lying at its rest pose. Nothing moves the arm or puts torque on it after that, so the gripper does not open and the arm is not folded: take out whatever is in the gripper yourself. At the other end the arm is still holding whatever it ended on, so it is handed back to you before anything opens: take hold of what is in the gripper and press Enter, the gripper opens all the way, and 3 seconds later the arm folds back to the rest pose and the gripper closes again, with a Ctrl-C or `q` holding it where it is. Leave it alone and it folds up with the gripper still shut. This needs the rest pose from step 6, because the rest pose is the one place Roboglot will drop torque and an arm released anywhere else falls, and it needs a terminal, because somebody has to press Enter. ```bash roboglot run --goal "draw a circle on the paper in front of you" --robot arm-01 --by-hand ``` **Give it a picture.** `--image` hands a file to the task itself, which is not the same thing as what the robot can see. The pilot gets each picture on its first turn, labelled with the file's own name, and keeps it in front of it for the whole run. That is what makes it different from a camera frame: a frame is perception, it arrives again every step and it shows the room as it is now, while a task picture never changes and is what the task is about. The flag repeats, so a run can carry several. It needs a pilot that takes images, `roboglot list-models` marks the LLMs that take no frames, and a local LLM needs `--vision`. ```bash roboglot run --goal "draw what is in the picture" --robot arm-01 --image sketch.png ``` **Or put a stepper in front of the pilot LLM.** `--decision-llm` is optional, off unless you name one, and needs no change to any of the ten steps above. With `--decision-mode shadow` a run is exactly the run it would have been, and the transcript also records what the decision LLM would have chosen on each turn, which is how you find out whether it is worth switching on for your bench. With `--decision-mode on` it answers the turns whose answer is a choice among calls the arm already has, and every joint angle is still the pilot LLM's. `jev` is TypeSafe's hosted one and wants `roboglot[decision]` and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` ([docs/guides/decision-llms/jev.md](docs/guides/decision-llms/jev.md)), `openai` is OpenAI's Decisions API and wants the `roboglot[openai]` and `OPENAI_API_KEY` a pilot through OpenAI already has ([docs/guides/decision-llms/openai.md](docs/guides/decision-llms/openai.md)), and every other name Roboglot knows, what it wants and where it runs, is one table in [docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md](docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md), a page each. ```bash roboglot run arm-grip-check --robot arm-01 --by-hand --decision-llm jev --decision-mode shadow ``` Put the two together and you have the drawing case: you set the arm down holding a pen where the paper is, and the LLM is looking at the sketch it has to copy. ```bash roboglot run --goal "draw what is in the picture" --robot arm-01 --image sketch.png --by-hand ``` **Two of those steps were not taken in the recording at the top of this page.** The run in that GIF was reached as `--robot lerobot:real --address COM3`, with no registered name and no rest pose. Step 5 existed that day and simply was not used. Step 6 did not exist at all: the rest pose was written after that afternoon, in answer to it. Both were taken on the same arm on 2026-09-23, and the rest pose could not be reached there, because the arm's calibration had never seen the shoulder folded all the way back and the fold lay past its travel. What Roboglot does with a fold like that now, and why step 3 asks you to calibrate folded, is [A pose past the travel](docs/adapters/lerobot/README.md#a-pose-past-the-travel). That has been exercised against `lerobot:mock` and in the test suite, and not yet on the arm. The arm in the recording is held up by torque alone, which is why it fell when the run ended. The two options after step 10 postdate that afternoon as well, and `--by-hand` and `--image` have both been exercised against `lerobot:mock` and in the test suite, and not yet on a real arm. Walk all ten and you are the second person down this path, so what differs on your bench is the part worth writing down. Two of the others change. Step 1 needs no pilot extra, so it is `uv pip install "roboglot[lerobot]"` on its own, and step 2 goes away, because Roboglot picks no LLM in this mode and reads no key. The LLM you are already chatting with is the pilot, so there is no `--llm` here at all. Steps 9 and 10 become one thing: point your client at the arm, then ask it in the chat. In Claude Code that is one command, and what it names is the `roboglot` inside the venv from step 1, by its absolute path. ```bash claude mcp add arm -- D:\Development\lerobot-test\.venv\Scripts\roboglot.exe serve-mcp --robot arm-01 ``` That path is a Windows one, and elsewhere it is the same venv's `bin/roboglot`. Use the venv rather than `uvx`, which builds a second environment on whichever interpreter it picks: on a machine whose default Python is 3.11 the LeRobot half of that extra resolves to nothing, silently, and you get a server with no arm backend in it. Claude Desktop takes the same command and arguments in `claude_desktop_config.json`, under Settings, then Developer, then Edit Config, and wants a full restart of the app afterwards. Either way nine `robot_*` tools appear, and behind them is the executor the rest of this page describes: the same allowlist, the same budgets, the same feasibility verdict before anything moves, and the same refusal for a joint goal outside the range your calibration recorded. What you gain over a `--goal` run is that you choose each verb and each number yourself, which is the only way to ask for one verb and stop, and the only way to ask a real arm for a camera frame on purpose. Two things are worth knowing before the first session. Starting the server moves the arm, because connecting drives it to the rest pose from step 6 and refuses to start at all if it cannot get there, so nobody should be in reach when a client spawns it. And there is no Ctrl-C: between verbs the brake is asking for `stop`, and during one it is the power switch. ## Why? A modern robot is not short of skills. The Microduck's onboard controllers already balance it, walk, kick, sit and scoop with its beak, and Pollen says its newest walking policy gets the duck back up after a fall. An arm picks with its own learned policy, a wheeled base drives. Each is the robot's own skill, trained, written or recorded, and each works without any help from an LLM. What the robot lacks is any idea of **what those skills are for**. ``` Traditional control: walk forward, turn left, walk, look down, scoop, ... (you plan every step) One robot: "Pick up the ball." (you state the goal) A team of them: "Pick up the ball." (they also settle who does it) ``` Low level skills and high level goals are different layers. The robot knows the words, but it cannot hold a conversation. Roboglot is an open source attempt to connect the two layers, with an LLM doing the planning and the robot's own controllers doing the moving. **The second gap opens with the second robot.** Every body speaks its own protocol, the arm's SDK, the cart's ZeroMQ host, the base's ROS topics, and every body has a different set of skills, so the robots you own end up commanded from as many terminals as there are robots and none of them knows the others exist. Roboglot puts them behind one command line, under names you choose, and lets one goal go to several of them at once. Each robot's pilot is told what the others are and what they can do, so the work gets divided on data rather than on guesses.
## How it works (the simple version) ```mermaid flowchart TD YOU["You
“find the ball and kick it”"] LLM["LLM
looks at the camera, the robot's state and the last result
picks ONE of the robot's own skills (a verb) and its parameters"] Q["Roboglot
checks the rules: allowed? task judged possible? budget left? needs confirmation?
then runs the verb"] R["Robot
executes the skill with its own controllers
(walking, grasping and looking are not the LLM's job)"] O["Roboglot observes the result
new camera frame, new state"] YOU --> LLM --> Q --> R --> O O -- "next verb, until done or impossible" --> LLM ``` The verbs the LLM can pick from are the robot's real, existing capabilities and nothing more. They come from its manifest, and a verb that is not in the manifest does not exist: | Kind | Verbs | What they are | |---|---|---| | Core | `observe` `report_state` `stop` `say` `move` `go_to` `search_scan` `approach_and` `map` `mark_place` `forget_place` `go_to_place` | on any robot whose manifest satisfies their requirements (a camera, a twist intent, a sound intent). The last four name the spots a robot stood on, list them and walk back to them, on a robot whose connection says where it is: a Microduck by its own odometry, a MOSS rover and a rosbridge base by theirs, and the mocks of all three ([docs/concepts/places.md](docs/concepts/places.md)) | | Microduck | `sit` `stand` `stand_up` `kick` `grab` `gaze` `quack` `watch` | one each per behaviour the robot ships with, each an *intent* the robot's own controllers execute. `watch` is Roboglot's own reflex and moves the head alone: it keeps something you describe in view for up to 30 seconds by asking a decision LLM that can see where it is in each camera frame, and it is there only on a run started with `--decision-llm openai --decision-frames`, and on a real duck only through mediad's `/frame` ([docs/adapters/microduck/README.md](docs/adapters/microduck/README.md#watch-a-head-that-keeps-something-in-view)). | | LeRobot arm | `move_joints` `gripper` `place` `pick` `manipulate` | an SO-101 class arm. `pick` and `manipulate` are each one skill intent the arm's own learned policy executes, confirm gated and present when a run names a policy server with `--policy-url`, and always on the mock, which scripts its own. `manipulate` hands it one short subtask and never says the task is done | | rosbridge base | `introspect` | a wheeled base over ROS 2. It gets `move`, `stop` and `report_state`, plus `observe`, `go_to`, `search_scan` and `approach_and` once an image topic is configured. `introspect` asks the bridge what the body is: the topic list and the robot's own description, which is where its weight and its joint count come from | | Open Duck Mini v2 | `gaze` `express` `quack` | a 42 cm biped. No `sit`, no `kick`, no `stand_up`: its runtime has no such skill, so the verb does not exist rather than being refused | | XLeRobot | `move_joints` `gripper` | a dual-arm cart. The arm joints are a normalised -100..100 range, not degrees, and `gripper` takes a `side` because there are two of them | | AlohaMini | `lift` `move_joints` `gripper` `home_arms` | two arms on a motorised lift. The arm verbs refuse until Roboglot's own host wrapper is running on the robot, because upstream's leaves the arms limp | | ToddlerBot | `look` `stand` `perform` `grip` | a humanoid. `look` turns a two joint neck, `stand` slews to the safe pose and is not a way up from a fall, and `perform` plays only the keyframe motions the daemon actually loaded. `grip` appears on the gripper builds, which carry two more motors | | Huebot | `sit` `stand` `stand_up` `kick` `quack` | a 25 cm biped whose maker is writing a shim for it that is to answer the Microduck's protocol, so these are the Microduck's verbs without `gaze` and `watch`, since the shim does not answer `robot.look` yet, and without `grab`, which waits for its maker to say what `ground_pick` does on Huebot. `sit`, `stand` and `kick` are there only when the shim lists the skill each one sends ([docs/adapters/huebot/README.md](docs/adapters/huebot/README.md)) | | MOSS | `drive_to` `explore` `pick_and_drop` `stow_arm` `collect_litter` | a small tracked rover that picks up litter, reached through its own cockpit and a bridge Roboglot ships for the rover. `drive_to` and `explore` hand a goal or a few minutes to MOSS's own planner and explorer, `pick_and_drop` and `stow_arm` play the maker's fixed arm cycle, which reaches for nothing, and `collect_litter` gives the rover to MOSS's own litter mission. It is the one `dangerous` verb, and it runs once per stack start ([docs/adapters/moss/README.md](docs/adapters/moss/README.md)) | | Industrial arm on ROS 2 | `move_joints` | a UR5e, a KUKA LBR iisy or iiwa or a Yaskawa MotoMini, through its ROS 2 driver and rosbridge, rehearsed only. `move_joints` sends one goal to every joint, at most at a tenth of each joint's rated speed at its fastest, and asks a person first every time: on `rosarm:mock` `--yes` may answer for them, and on `rosarm:ws` it does not. No gripper and no `pick`: Roboglot drives no tool, and it never powers, enables or un-brakes an arm ([docs/adapters/rosarm/README.md](docs/adapters/rosarm/README.md)) | | Aliases | `get_frame` `walk_to` `walk` | the 0.3 names of `observe`, `go_to` and `move`. They keep working in every `.glot` file | | Learned | *(none yet)* | v2: policies trained from LLM written rewards, registered like any other verb. The arm's `pick` and `manipulate` do run a learned policy, and they are the arm's own verbs rather than these ([docs/guides/policies.md](docs/guides/policies.md)) | `go_to` (still spelled `walk_to` in the older starter files) is a small closed loop in plain Python that steers toward whatever the camera sees, ten times a second, without asking the LLM. The LLM says *"go to the ball"* and never *"turn 4° left"*. The same code steers a duck, a cart and a wheeled base, clamped to each manifest's speed limits. On a body with no locomotion, such as the arm, `go_to` does not exist at all. On the ToddlerBot, which looks with a two joint neck, `search_scan` sweeps the head instead of turning the body. A team is that same loop once per robot, all at once, with a bus between the pilots so one can tell another what it is about to do ([Team mode](#team-mode)).
## Example An `open-duck-scout` run on the Open Duck Mini's mock, from its transcript (`runs/-open-duck-scout/transcript.jsonl`). The mock draws an orange ball for the duck's camera, so `go_to` has something to steer at. Every run opens the same way, with the pilot judging whether this body can do this task at all, because nothing that moves the duck runs until it has. This one is the scripted pilot, so `llm_id` says so, the verdict says a rule has no judgement of a body, and `usage` is an estimate from character counts (no tokenizer). A real provider records the API's own counts and weighs the task against the datasheet in its prompt. ```jsonc {"kind": "llm", "step": 0, "tool_calls": [{"name": "assess_task", "arguments": {"verdict": "feasible", "reason": "scripted pilot: a rule has no judgement of the body, so it assumes the task fits"}}], "usage": {"input_tokens": 1658, "output_tokens": 16}} {"kind": "assess", "step": 0, "verdict": "feasible", "reason": "scripted pilot: a rule has no judgement of the body, so it assumes the task fits"} {"kind": "llm", "step": 0, "tool_calls": [{"name": "go_to", "arguments": {"target": "ball", "stop_distance": 0.3}}]} {"kind": "verb", "step": 1, "name": "go_to", "ok": true, "summary": "reached the ball: ~0.28 m away, bearing +0°", "data": {"distance_m": 0.278, "bearing_deg": 0.0, "ticks": 53}} {"kind": "llm", "step": 1, "tool_calls": [{"name": "say", "arguments": {"text": "ball at 0 degrees left, about 0.3 m"}}]} {"kind": "verb", "step": 2, "name": "say", "ok": true, "summary": "said 'ball at 0 degrees left, about 0.3 m' as [chirp]"} {"kind": "llm", "step": 2, "tool_calls": [{"name": "declare_success", "arguments": {"reason": "walked up and reported"}}]} ``` The same thing as a conversation, through MCP in Claude Code or Claude Desktop: > **You:** List the duck's verbs, then find the ball, walk up to it and say where it is. > **Claude:** *(calls `robot_list_verbs`, `robot_observe`, `robot_assess_task("feasible")`, `robot_run_verb("go_to")`, `robot_say`)* Done. I walked up to the ball and said where it is. And the same shape with two robots instead of one, from the `team.jsonl` of a `team-hello` run: the duck's mock and the arm's, one pilot each, on wall clock. Nothing here moves a joint on purpose, because this is the smallest honest test that two pilots in two different bodies can find each other and exchange a fact. ```jsonc {"t": 0.94, "kind": "bus", "msg": {"src": "duck", "kind": "TALK", "to": null, "text": "duck here and ready; say hello back"}} {"t": 1.048, "kind": "bus", "msg": {"src": "arm", "kind": "TALK", "to": null, "text": "arm here and ready; say hello back"}} {"t": 1.145, "kind": "member_end", "robot": "arm", "outcome": "success", "reason": "said hello and heard back from duck", "llm_calls": 3} {"t": 1.147, "kind": "bus", "msg": {"src": "team", "kind": "TALK", "to": null, "text": "arm declared success: said hello and heard back from duck"}} {"t": 1.309, "kind": "member_end", "robot": "duck", "outcome": "success", "reason": "said hello and heard back from arm", "llm_calls": 4} {"t": 1.31, "kind": "bus", "msg": {"src": "team", "kind": "TALK", "to": null, "text": "duck declared success: said hello and heard back from arm"}} {"t": 1.318, "kind": "team_end", "outcome": "success", "reason": "every member declared success: duck, arm", "messages": 2, "llm_calls": 7} ``` `tell` is what put the first two lines on the bus. It moves nothing, costs no step, and arrives in the addressee's next observation. Each member then declared for itself, the runner put a line of its own on the bus as `team` each time to tell the other, and the team succeeds only when all of them did. This one is the scripted pilot again, so the sentences are a rule's and not an LLM's.

Local setup, tool calling flags per server and what to expect from small LLMs: [docs/guides/local-llms.md](docs/guides/local-llms.md). Over MCP there is no `--llm` at all. `roboglot serve-mcp` selects no LLM, and the chat client's own LLM is the pilot ([docs/guides/mcp.md](docs/guides/mcp.md)). ### Decision LLMs **Decision LLMs are not in the pilots' table on purpose.** A decision LLM is not a provider and `--llm` does not take one: it answers typed questions about a state and writes nothing, so it cannot pilot a robot on its own. It sits in front of whichever provider you did pick, for the turns whose answer is a choice, it is named with `--decision-llm` instead, and it is off unless you name one ([docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md](docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md)). There are seven, `jev` and `openai` hosted by their makers, `kev`, `openjev` and `opendecision` servers you run yourself, `local` for any other server that speaks the same wire format, and `laya` in Roboglot's own process. Try one in shadow first, where it is asked every turn and changes nothing, and the run's record says what it would have answered: ```bash roboglot run arm-grip-check --robot lerobot:mock --llm openai --decision-llm jev --decision-mode shadow ``` Each one's key, extra, address and rate are in [docs/models/decision-llms.md](docs/models/decision-llms.md). ### Learned policies and VLAs No vendor serves many VLAs per call the way OpenRouter serves many LLMs, so Roboglot's answer is Hugging Face: LeRobot's checkpoints on the Hub, served by Roboglot's own policy server, which reads each family's code before it serves it and refuses the rest before a byte of weights is fetched. It serves ACT, SmolVLA, Physical Intelligence's pi05 and pi0, X-VLA in the arm's own joints and NVIDIA's GR00T N1.7, and refuses pi0-FAST, whose policy runs its tokenizer's code from the Hub. The server runs in a process of its own, never in the one that owns the arm's serial bus: on the laptop, on a GPU you rent and tunnel to, or on a Hugging Face Inference Endpoint, a GPU that Roboglot starts for you and Hugging Face bills by the hour. ```bash uv pip install "roboglot[lerobot-vla]" # where the policy runs, Python 3.12 roboglot policy serve --policy OWNER/NAME@REVISION # on this machine, or on a GPU you rent roboglot policy endpoint up arm --policy OWNER/NAME@REVISION # or on a Hugging Face GPU, by the hour roboglot run task.glot --robot arm-01 --llm openai --policy-url hf:arm # the arm, its segments from the endpoint ``` The endpoint asks before it bills, waits until the server answers, pauses itself when it fails, and `roboglot policy endpoint pause arm` stops the bill. Roboglot has never created one: it has run against the test suite's stand-ins alone. What each family needs, its licence, where it runs and what is not served and why are in [docs/models/vlas.md](docs/models/vlas.md), and setting one up is [docs/guides/policies.md](docs/guides/policies.md).
## Architecture Three loops, three rates, three owners. The LLM decides **what**, at 0.2 to 1 Hz. The steering loop decides **how to get there**, at 10 Hz, and never waits for the LLM. The robot's own controllers do the **moving**, at their own rate: balance on a biped, a pick policy on an arm, a gait policy on a humanoid, the driver on a wheeled base. The table with the rates and the owners is in [docs/concepts/architecture.md](docs/concepts/architecture.md). The robot is an *adapter* that declares a *manifest*: what body it has, which intents and sensors, which verbs, what stops it. The registry, the tool list, the verbs a `.glot` may allow and the system prompt are built from that manifest when the robot connects. A verb that is not in it does not exist. All ten bodies go through the same loop, executor and contract ([ADR-0017](docs/adr/0017-robot-adapters-and-manifest.md)). Each adapter is also a distribution of its own, written in [`adapters/`](adapters/) here and installed beside the core as `roboglot_`, so the only robot code on your machine is the robot you own. A team of pilots is that whole stack once per robot, side by side, with one bus between the pilots and one kill switch that reaches every executor. ```mermaid flowchart LR HUMAN["Human

The **body** is data, one per robot: its manifest, datasheet, verbs, limits, safety authority, rest pose and what it cannot do. Of the four layers it is the only one the LLM reads, beside the task and what the robot remembers, and a [described body](docs/adapters/status.md#described-bodies) is nothing else. A **behaviour family** is what bodies of a kind do alike: an arm folds before it lets go, and a biped's runtime is kept fed with twists while it walks. Its code is shared once two bodies need it, and not before: the Microduck and Huebot are one set of verbs and one transport under two body records, and every other body is a package of its own. A **binding** is how an intent reaches the robot, by one of three routes: an SDK Roboglot imports, a wire protocol it speaks, or a bridge it ships for the robot's own computer. The **transport** under that moves bytes and knows nothing about the body. So the next robot that speaks a protocol a package already speaks costs a body and not a whole adapter ([ADR-0075](docs/adr/0075-an-adapter-is-a-family-a-body-file-and-a-binding.md)).


Only the body layer is one per robot. Below it each robot sits in the box of its kind and the box of its route. Each robot is drawn where its row in the adapter catalogue puts it, by docs/assets/architecture.py, so a new one joins the picture without anyone redrawing it.

**Why predefined skills matter.** The LLM never generates motor commands. Every verb is an *intent* the robot already understands: a velocity, a named skill (`kick_left` or `ground_pick` on the Microduck, `pick` as a LeRobot policy on the arm), a gaze target, a sound, a joint goal, a gripper command. The robot's own controllers do the physical part, on the Microduck policies trained in [microduck_rl](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck_rl) and exported to ONNX at 50 Hz, so a slow or confused LLM degrades the *task*, never the *balance*. Where a body has a deadman it stops itself when commands stall. The Microduck's `robotd` has one, Huebot's shim is asked to keep the same, which nobody has seen it do, on the Open Duck and the ToddlerBot the daemon Roboglot ships is the deadman, the XLeRobot's and the AlohaMini's hosts stop the wheels but not the arms, and on the arm and a rosbridge base Roboglot's heartbeat and `stop` are the only stop authority. The LLM names the skill, the body performs it. **Enforcement order.** Every verb call passes `Executor.run_verb`, which applies the contract in a fixed order: abort flag, allowlist, the pilot's feasibility verdict, parameter validation, budgets, `abort_when`, preconditions, and only then the confirm gate, so nobody is asked about a call a gate before it would refuse, then everything that can change while a person is asked read again on a new reading of the body's state, dry run, then execution with a timeout that races the abort, so a kill switch cancels the verb that is running. The preconditions are named by the manifest and supplied by the adapter, so a body's own rules are its own: not fallen on a duck, torque on and a cool servo for an arm, calibrated and not fallen on the humanoid. The full order and what each step means: [docs/concepts/safety.md](docs/concepts/safety.md). **Prompts.** The system prompt opens with the robot's own one line introduction from its manifest, then the contract in prose, what the robot remembers from earlier runs, and the `.glot` body verbatim. Tools are JSON schemas generated from each verb's parameter model, plus `assess_task`, `declare_success` and `declare_failure`, plus `remember` when memory is on and `tell` when the run is a team of pilots, and the pilot LLM must return exactly one tool call. Only the last two observations keep their images, and up to the last nine on `--llm anthropic` with one of the Claude LLMs that bind their thinking (Opus 5.5, Fable 5.2, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.1), whose old frames are trimmed every eight exchanges rather than on every one. Local LLMs get one extra line describing the JSON shape to answer with when native tool calling is unavailable. The system prompt and the tools that are not verbs are in [`roboglot/agent/prompts.py`](roboglot/agent/prompts.py). **An optional stepper in front of the pilot LLM.** `--decision-llm` lets a decision LLM take the turns whose answer is a choice among calls this body already has. It is a different kind of LLM rather than a cheaper one of the same kind: it emits no tokens, so where a pilot LLM writes you a verb and Roboglot parses it, a decision LLM scores the verbs you gave it and hands back which one with a probability for each, and there is nowhere in that answer for a number to come from. [TypeSafe's Jev](https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction) was the first and gave the wire format its name ([docs/guides/decision-llms/jev.md](docs/guides/decision-llms/jev.md)), and what most of the others share with it is that format rather than a vendor, so each is a row of data with a page of its own, and `--decision-llm local --decision-url` reaches anything else that answers `POST /v1/systemone`. OpenAI's Decisions API asks the same kind of question in a format of its own, `POST /v1/decisions`, so `--decision-llm openai` has a client of its own that translates it ([docs/guides/decision-llms/openai.md](docs/guides/decision-llms/openai.md)). The stepper sits inside *think* and nowhere else: no adapter knows about it, the executor is unchanged, and which verbs it may answer is computed from each tool's own JSON schema, so a verb with a number in it is never one of them. It is off unless a run names one, and a turn it answers never enters the pilot LLM's history, because none of it is anything the pilot LLM said. [docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md](docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md) and [ADR-0040](docs/adr/0040-a-discrete-stepper-in-front-of-the-pilot-llm.md). A decision LLM that can see has one more place, inside one verb rather than in front of the pilot LLM: on a Microduck, `--decision-frames` gives the pilot `watch`, which asks it where a thing the pilot described is in each camera frame, and turns the head by Roboglot's own arithmetic, so the decision LLM says where the thing is and never how far to turn ([ADR-0054](docs/adr/0054-a-reflex-may-look-through-a-decision-llm.md)). **Perception: features, not frames.** The default detector is an HSV colour threshold, a few milliseconds per frame, no model download. Bearing comes from horizontal position through the camera's focal length. Distance comes from apparent size, so `--fov-deg` matters on a real camera. It looks for one orange ball, in the orange the mocks that draw a ball paint it, so it works on them out of the box. For a real ball you tune one HSV range ([FAQ](docs/faq.md)). A YOLO detector is an optional extra, in this process with `--detector yolo` or on a Jetson's GPU with `--detector host`, and a real body run with `--host` uses the board's by default when that board can detect. **Talking to the robots.** Each adapter speaks its body's own protocol and spells every upstream name in one `upstream_api.py`, tagged VERIFIED (read from upstream source at a pinned commit) or UNVERIFIED, and a test proves the unverified ones are only reachable from the experimental backends. Two bodies are reached through an installed SDK (the arm through LeRobot, the base through roslibpy), two by speaking the ZeroMQ host they already ship because neither is an installable package (the XLeRobot and the AlohaMini), and two through a daemon Roboglot ships for the robot because neither runtime has a network API at all (the Open Duck Mini and the ToddlerBot). The Microduck's `robotd` speaks JSON RPC 2.0 over a unix socket, and Roboglot re-sends `robot.move` every 100 ms while walking on purpose, because the robot zeroes its velocity when those stop. Huebot's own API is closed, so its maker is writing a shim for it that is to answer that same protocol. Each body's page under [docs/adapters/](docs/adapters/) carries its VERIFIED and UNVERIFIED tables, and the traps that recur when you read a robot you cannot run are collected in [docs/adapters/reading-robots.md](docs/adapters/reading-robots.md). **Safety layer.** Heartbeat failure, Ctrl+C and `q` all mean the same thing: `stop`, then abort. A verb that times out or raises stops the robot and comes back as a failed result, not an abort. `--dry-run` sends nothing. And `stop` always means stop, never collapse, on every body: Roboglot sends no robot's go limp call, ever. Session end is different on the arm, where LeRobot's own `disconnect()` releases torque by its default, which is what dropped the arm at the end of every run on the bench. So an arm with a [rest pose](#your-robots-by-name) recorded is driven back to it between the stop and the disconnect, on every exit path there is, and when it cannot get there Roboglot leaves torque on and says so rather than letting the arm fall. What actually stops each body when Roboglot goes quiet differs enough to be worth a table of its own, and each manifest declares its own answer in `safety_authority`: [docs/concepts/safety.md](docs/concepts/safety.md). The full map, with a "why it exists" line per module: [docs/concepts/architecture.md](docs/concepts/architecture.md). Decisions and their reasons: [docs/adr/](docs/adr/).
## Installation Requirements: Python 3.11 or newer and [`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/). Windows, macOS and Linux. No GPU needed: Roboglot's core touches none. Every Roboglot command but one runs on your laptop and reaches an NVIDIA Jetson's LLM server, camera and detector over the network with `--host` ([docs/guides/jetson.md](docs/guides/jetson.md)). The one that runs on a robot's own computer is `roboglot onboard`, [Robot Passport](#robot-passport)'s service, which can drive the robot from there as well, and a Jetson is its first board, though nothing of it has run on one yet. The core is about 120 MB and it is the loop, the executor and the contract, with no robot in it. **`uv pip install roboglot` installs no robot.** You choose the body next, and each of the ten is its own package on PyPI (`roboglot-microduck`, `roboglot-lerobot` and eight more) that the extra of the same name pulls in. Until one of them is installed, every command that needs a body refuses and says what to install. ```bash uvx roboglot --version # the core on its own: the loop, the executor, the contract uv pip install "roboglot[microduck]" # then a body: or lerobot, rosbridge, open_duck, xlerobot, alohamini, toddlerbot, huebot, moss, rosarm uv pip install "roboglot[robots]" # or all ten at once, each with the SDK its real backend needs uv pip install "roboglot[microduck-camera]" # the duck plus its WebRTC camera uv pip install "roboglot[lerobot-vla]" # the arm's policy server: LeRobot, torch and transformers, Python 3.12 uv pip install "roboglot[ui]" # the page in a browser or on a phone, roboglot ui: Streamlit uv tool install "roboglot[onboard]" # on a robot's own computer: roboglot onboard, Robot Passport, with --python 3.12 on JetPack 6 uv pip install "roboglot[anthropic]" # the brain: or openai, gemini, grok, mistral, deepseek, cohere, qwen, kimi, glm, meta, openrouter, all git clone https://github.com/rokbenko/quackd && cd Roboglot && uv sync # contributors: the core and all ten adapters, editable ``` The extras are independent and they compose, so a body and a brain are one install (`uv pip install "roboglot[microduck,anthropic]"`) or none at all (`uvx --from "roboglot[microduck,anthropic]" roboglot run ...`). `roboglot[lerobot]` installs anywhere and reaches a real arm only on Python 3.12 or newer, because LeRobot itself does: below that floor the marker resolves to no SDK and you are left with `lerobot:mock`, which is why `roboglot doctor` is where you check rather than the install output. `roboglot[lerobot-vla]` is the arm's policy server, `roboglot policy serve`, which needs LeRobot and Python 3.12 and belongs wherever the policy runs rather than in the process that drives the arm ([docs/guides/policies.md](docs/guides/policies.md)). And `roboglot[yolo]`, `roboglot[lan]` and `roboglot[ui]` are the other detector, LAN discovery and the page `roboglot ui` serves. `roboglot[decision]` is the System One client for the optional discrete stepper and `roboglot[laya]` is the one that runs in this process instead of behind a server. Both are off unless a run names a decision LLM, and neither is part of `roboglot[all]`, deliberately, because a stepper nobody asked for should never be installed by asking for everything. `--decision-llm openai` needs neither, because its client is the `openai` SDK the pilot already uses ([docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md](docs/guides/decision-llms/README.md)). `roboglot[onboard]` goes on a robot's own computer, and on a laptop for the `sim` board and its demo: `roboglot onboard` with zeroconf, an OpenAI-compatible client for the robot's brain and, on Linux alone, the Bluetooth libraries, and it is not part of `roboglot[all]` either. Which body a command means when you do not name one is in [Configuration](#configuration), and `roboglot doctor` says what this machine has. **What a version promises.** The eleven packages always ship together, with one version. While Roboglot is 0.x, a patch, the third number, fixes what Roboglot did not do the way its docs or its own output said, and asks nothing of a setup that worked, except where a safety fix refuses something the docs never promised, which its note then says. A minor, the second number, may add, change or remove a command, a flag, a default or a file format, and its note says what to do. So a requirement that allows one minor takes every fix to it and nothing new. [RELEASING.md](RELEASING.md) has the whole rule.
## Usage ```bash # a goal in human language (a wheeled base's mock, scripted pilot, no key needed) uvx --from "roboglot[rosbridge]" roboglot run --goal "walk in a square" --robot rosbridge:mock --llm fake # the same goal with Claude uvx --from "roboglot[rosbridge,anthropic]" roboglot run --goal "walk in a square" --robot rosbridge:mock --llm anthropic # a task file (seventeen ship with the core, the starter table below lists them) uvx --from "roboglot[microduck]" roboglot run hello-world --llm fake ``` Every run writes `runs/-/` (`--runs-dir` replaces `runs/`, and `--run-name "Example 1"` adds your own label to the end of that directory, `runs/20260921-155518-find-and-kick-example-1/`) with `transcript.jsonl` (every prompt, tool call, gate, intent, result and token count, what each LLM call cost and what the run has cost so far, when the run started and when it ended, plus the robot's manifest in `run_start`), every frame Roboglot captured, `summary.json`, `terminal.txt` (everything that was on the terminal during the run, as plain text, opening with the command that started it and the version that ran it). `roboglot log` replays any of it afterwards. Cloud or local, same command.
